why_a_second_file_and_not_an_edit_of_A3s: Editing docs/conformance/oc-axes-2026-07-28.json would give one artefact two owners — the MES-24 two-censuses defect, where the two disagree and nothing detects it. axis_source_rule: AXES COME FROM THE PREDICATE, NEVER FROM THE DESCRIPTION — docs/conformance/match-relation.md §2, cited not restated.
difference_from_A3s_13: A3's 13 are all `a(...)`-form checks whose predicate is an inline arrow function, so every axis expression is a substring of the emitting excerpt itself. NONE of the checks here is like that: every one computes its predicate into a minified binding BEFORE the emitting call, and three of them are decided at a site that is not the emitting site at all. C1b-ii's 9 are the sharpest case — their verdict is `i.length===0` / `o.length===0` over an error accumulator filled by a ternary several hundred bytes earlier, so EVERY axis expr lives in a `context_excerpt` and none in the evaluator excerpt. So each row carries `context_excerpts` — further addressed spans the predicate depends on — and an axis `expr` is a verbatim substring of the evaluator excerpt OR of one of them. The row says which, in `expr_found_in`.

provenance.emitting_spans_from: docs/conformance/oc-emitting-sites-2026-07-28.json — generated by mix conformance.locator, not re-cut by hand
provenance.context_spans_from: located by unique-substring search against the same build; each is unique in it
provenance.bytes_are_not_stored_here: Spans only. `mix conformance.crosswalk` lifts the bytes LIVE from the build at these spans and refuses if any axis `expr` is not a verbatim substring of what it lifted. Storing the bytes here as well would create a second copy that can drift from the build without anything noticing — the same reasoning bucket-0 gives for lifting rather than remembering.

polarity_rule: `pass_when_true` — the expression being TRUE is the passing arm. `fail_when_true` — the expression being TRUE is the failing arm. Read off the branch the excerpt actually writes, never off the requirement's wording.
preconditions_rule: A list of `{guard, kind, on_failure, reads}`. A precondition is NOT an axis, and the reason is NOT the status it writes: it is that the guard reads something OTHER than a behaviour of the implementation under test — the harness's own transport, whether a diagnostic tool is listed, whether the probe was run at all — so an ET claim can neither agree with it nor contradict it, and `shape_from_axes/1` never sees one. C1a stated the rule as `its failure makes the check not evaluate (SKIPPED)`, and C1c-i measured that that is NOT what the artefacts do: A3's own server-stateless rows record `()=>n?` and `()=>S?` and `!r||!i` as preconditions whose `on_failure` is an ERROR MESSAGE, and the check goes red. Three `on_failure` shapes occur in this file and each is written as what it is — `SKIPPED` (ServerIdentifiesInResultMeta's `if(_)return{skipped:!0`, and the two `listChanged` rows' capability guards), a FAILURE naming the probe, and a WARNING carrying `details:{untestable:!0}`. The rule as C1a wrote it would have forced a dozen harness-transport guards to be recorded as AXES, and every ET claim would then have been `silent` on them — which makes every red-OC edge `:partial` and bucket 4b by construction, and would have made A3 §3's `(red, green, :full)` escalation UNREACHABLE on the first leg where it can occur. Restating the rule on its actual ground is therefore not a loosening; it is what stops the decomposition deciding an adjudication.

context_excerpts.why: THE PREDICATE IS THE FILTER. `o` — the accumulator the emitting site reads as `o.length===0` — is `t.filter(e=>e.origin===`implementation`)`, so what the check scores is not `were there violations` but `were there violations ATTRIBUTED TO THE IMPLEMENTATION`

context_excerpts.why: holds the early `return[]` that decides whether this check is emitted at all

context_excerpts.label: harness_origin_sibling
context_excerpts.why: the `origin===`harness`` sibling, addressed so the SCOPE of this check is evidence and not inference: violations in messages the HARNESS sent are scored by `WireSchemaHarnessError`, never here

context_excerpts.label: input_requests_schema_definition
context_excerpts.why: the `$defs` entry this family's messages are validated AGAINST, addressed rather than paraphrased: `InputRequests` is `type: `object`` with `additionalProperties` a `$ref` to `InputRequest`. It is what makes this axis reachable from an ET claim about the SHAPE of `inputRequests`, and it is the only place in the crosswalk where the schema itself, rather than a check's predicate, decides a verdict

axes.polarity_reading: `o=t.filter(e=>e.origin===`implementation`)` then `status:o.length===0?`SUCCESS`:`FAILURE`` — a violation whose origin is the implementation is what fails it
axes.requires: every JSON-RPC message OUR side put on the wire during this scenario validates against the published spec schema for the negotiated version

checks.scope_note: ONE DIRECTION ONLY, and that is why this row carries the `harness_origin_sibling` excerpt. The filter scopes the check to messages the IMPLEMENTATION SENT. Nothing here scores what the implementation does with a message it RECEIVED — those violations carry `origin===`harness``, go to `WireSchemaHarnessError`, and that check is a bug report about the harness rather than a score of our parsing.
checks.why_fourteen_rows_share_one_site: FOURTEEN ROWS, ONE SITE, and this is a property of the artefacts rather than a choice made here. `WireSchemaValid` is emitted from a single generic validator (byte span [325368,325721]) that every scenario runs, so A1's six-field key — which carries the SCENARIO — makes fourteen distinct checks of it in this family alone, and G19 requires each of the fourteen to be decomposed before any of them can be reported in bucket 2. The decomposition is therefore the SAME reading fourteen times, and what actually differs row to row is the KEY and `status_at_accepted_run`. This is not the D4 defect it resembles: D4 forbids one FACT having two homes, and the fact here — `this check, in this scenario, decomposes to this axis` — is fourteen facts about fourteen keys. It is said plainly because fourteen near-identical rows otherwise read as a copy-paste nobody checked. C1b-iii's `client/tools_call` row is the fifteenth instance and is NOT touched: it is another ticket's and one fact has one home.
checks.what_the_schema_binds_here: For this family the binding definition is `InputRequests`, and it is ADDRESSED as this row's `input_requests_schema_definition` excerpt rather than quoted here. It is `type: `object``, so an `InputRequiredResult` whose `inputRequests` is a JSON ARRAY is a violation this axis is about — which is what makes this row reachable from an ET claim about the shape of `inputRequests` at all.

preconditions.on_failure: check_not_emitted
preconditions.reads: whether any message was observed at all; a run that validated nothing emits no check rather than a vacuous SUCCESS

emitting_span_provenance_rule: Every row states where its `emitting_byte_span` came from, and the generator CHECKS the statement against MES-97's locator output (G18). `locator_row` — the span is one the locator names for this row's key, and the generator requires that. `locator_row_rejected` — the locator's own `rung_pin_level` for that row is NOT `row`, so it does not claim to pin the row; the span it names belongs to a sibling and is refused. The generator then requires the reverse: the pin level must not be `row`, the span used must NOT be one of the locator's, and a reason must be given. Four of C1b-i's 29 rows are rejections; C1a's 11 are all `locator_row`, and were so before this field existed. C1b-ii's 9 are all `locator_row` TOO, and each carries an `emitting_span_provenance_why` anyway — not because G18 demands one on an acceptance (it does not), but because the locator pins these rows at level CHECK and names three sites for every one of them, so G18 would accept the Name push against a Method row and vice versa. The acceptance is honest and the residual it leaves is stated on the row rather than in this rule. C1b-iii's 4 are all `locator_row`, and ONE of them — DefaultResultTypeComplete — is the same shape again and carries its own `emitting_span_provenance_why`: the locator pins it at level CHECK and names FOUR sites, two of which are not this check's pushes at all but unrelated code binding some `i`. Saying so on the row is the whole remedy available here; G18 cannot distinguish them, and pretending otherwise would be the AC7 error. C1c-ii's 36 are all `locator_row` and none is a rejection: every row in the family is pinned by the locator at level `row` (the id literal sits beside the row's own name at every site), so the choice among a row's sites is between an EVALUATOR site and a `catch`-arm site that carries the same id — and this file takes the evaluator site in all 36. That is a reading the locator does not make for it, and it is the same residual C1b-ii recorded for the header rows rather than a new one.
check_id_location_rule: C1a's 11 rows all carry their check id as a backtick literal at the emitting site, and the generator required exactly that. Fourteen of C1b-i's rows emit with `id:c` — a value COMPUTED from the argument's value and declared type — and ten more with `id:t`, a loop variable. So a row may name `check_id_found_in`: the pool entry whose bytes must carry the id literal. It defaults to `evaluator_excerpt`, which is C1a's behaviour unchanged, and the named entry must exist. This WEAKENS the guard from `the id is at the emitting site` to `the id is verbatim at an ADDRESSED span this row names`, and that is said plainly rather than left to be noticed: what it still refuses is a row whose id occurs nowhere it points at. C1b-iii adds one more user of the field — DefaultResultTypeComplete, which emits with `id:i` where `i` is bound to the literal one statement earlier, so the literal is in the guard excerpt and nowhere near either push. C1c-i meets a third shape and it is the first that NO span can satisfy. The `server-stateless` RequestMetaInvalid trio emits with ``id:`sep-2575-request-meta-invalid-${e.slug}` `` and the composed ids occur NOWHERE in the build — measured, 0 hits each for `sep-2575-request-meta-invalid-missing-meta`, `-missing-protocol-version` and `-missing-client-capabilities` in the 809 KB dist — so `check_id_found_in` cannot help whichever span it names. Such a row states `check_id_composition` instead: a `template` verbatim at a named span, a `hole` occurring EXACTLY ONCE in it, and a `substitution` verbatim at another named span, with the substituted result required to equal the check id EXACTLY. The two fields are mutually exclusive — two answers to one question, and nothing would choose between them. This is NOT a further weakening: the literal form asks `is the id at a span you name`, and the composed form asks the same question of every PART of the id, with the template pinned to the build so the only freedom is the one hole. A row cannot cover the id with fragments it found lying around (the S9-18 shape), because a degenerate cover would have to be a template that is verbatim in the dist and contains the hole, which is the emitting site itself. C1c-ii adds no new user of either field: all 36 of its rows carry the check id as a backtick literal AT the emitting site, which is C1a's original behaviour, so all 36 take the `evaluator_excerpt` default. Recorded because a family of 36 landing entirely on the oldest and strictest form is worth stating — the weakenings above are not load-bearing here.
